newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai oil firms raise pump prices as baht plunges.
newsitem.headline: Thai oil firms raise pump prices as baht plunges.

text.p: Major Thai oil firms have raised pump prices to reflect higher costs as the baht plunged to another record low on Thursday, industry sources said.
State-run Petroleum Authority of Thailand, Bangchak Petroleum Plc, Caltex, Esso, and Shell all increased pump prices by 15 satangs (five US cents) after similar hikes in the past two weeks.
After the adjustments, PTT oil prices, viewed as the benchmark in the retail oil business, stood at 9.73 baht ($0.31) per litre for unleaded gasoline and 8.60 baht for diesel fuel.

Industry sources said the cost of oil production had risen as the baht weakened. The currency has lost more than 20 poercent of its value since July 2 when the authorities announced they were switching to managed float of the baht from a tightly-controlled exchange rate regime.
On Thursday, the baht tumbled to a new record low of 32.63 baht per dollar in a thin market makred by high commercial demand.
Dealers speculated that corporates bought the greenback to repay debt as some foreign financial institutions declined to roll over their loans as the economic problems intensified.
Prasert Boonsumpun, president of PTT Oil, told reporters that as the baht weakened to 30.00-31.00 baht, the cost of oil rose by 60 satangs per litre and diesel around 50 satangs.
"Even with the latest adjustment, we still have to shoulder extra cost. But we will adjust the retail prices in stages in best efforts to delay the effect on consumers," he said.
The government pledged it will not intervene to control oil prices to curb inflation after the baht's de facto devaluation. However, it had asked oil firms to raise prices gradually.
Caltex officials declined to forecast the future of prices, but said the company would try to maintain current prices for as long as possible.
"While we have still not entirely recovered the loss from the baht devaluation, we will try our best to maintain prices as long as possible," said the official.

"Since the oil price is composed of several factors -- exchange rate, crude price, and business expenses -- it is very difficult to forecast future prices. At the moment, selling prices are still lower than what they were earlier this year," she said,
An official at another major foreign oil firm said the biggest factor for oil prices now was the exchange rate, as international crude oil prices were holding steady.
North Sea Brent crude, the international benchmark, was quoted around US$18.41/18.45 per barrel for August/September. Dubai was quoted around $17.30/17.40 for nearby months.
However, the situation could worsen as western hemisphere winter arrives because crude prices usually rise then.
"If the economy fails to improve and boost sentiment on the baht by then, crude prices will jump and it could be an ugly scene," he said.
